about: The words of the chain saxon_exiles_804 (Data/encounters/chain_saxon_exiles_804_793.json; Design/content/chains/saxon_exiles_804.md): the last deportation of the Saxon war, 804, and one family of Wihmodia at the Ems mouth. Every title, intention, line and label key of its fourteen cards; an outcome text for every option (keys '...out_<option>', and '...out_<option>_success' and '..._failure' where there is a chance; named in each option's note: the engine shows the effects' own facts, the outcome texts are for the integrator); the two news items the cards post; and one 'art.<card id>' line for each card's picture. People: Tetta and Folcger are places/emuthon.json; Liudger is the spine's cast.liudger; King Godfred (cast.godfred) is named and not met. Meginward, Aldburg, Ricswind, Folcward, Gerburg, Meginfrid and the count's man Gundhart are ordinary invented people. Nothing is quoted: the annal of 804, Einhard and the baptismal vow are given in our own plain words. Written 6 Oct 2026; a draft for the user to overwrite.

entries.text: The people on the bank

Some hundreds of people sit on the river bank with spearmen walking round them: Saxons, with their children, their old people and what they could carry. Nobody is tied. There is nowhere to run to. An officer of the host walks along the boats, asking for hulls.
Shipman. I have four hundred heads to put over the river and one ferry with a split plank. Two pennies a head, counted in and counted out.

They are the emperor's Saxons, from Wihmodia and from over the Elbe. They go into Francia, a few here and a few there, where there is nobody to rise with. Thirty years of war, and this is how it ends: on foot.
The emperor sits by the Elbe this summer with the whole host. The land beyond it is to be empty before Michaelmas, and the Wends are to have it. Ask me again who won.
These are the last. The ones who sat out the winter in the woods and came in when the snow did the count's work for him.

Frisian. You go down the river and along the coast. My sister Aldburg and her man did not come in to be counted. They said the Ems, and then the Danes. If you see them, say Ricburg lives, and went west.
Take the officer's hire and carry a boatload over
Buy bread and have it carried down the line
Say your hold is full, and stand and look

Twelve of them at a time, two crossings. They sit where they are put and hold the children by the wrist. A woman in the second load says a name to you, Aldburg, and a river, the Ems. The officer counts them out on the far bank and pays in new pennies, twenty-four.

The baker's boy carries the baskets down the line and the spearmen let him. Nobody thanks you. One woman breaks her loaf in three, looks at you over it, and says a name, Aldburg, and a river, the Ems.

The officer shrugs and goes on to the next boat. You stand and look for as long as it takes to see that it is a whole country sitting there. A woman by the water calls something to you in Saxon about her sister and the Ems.

A wide river bank in flat afternoon light: some hundreds of Saxons sitting on the grass with bundles, children and old people, a loose ring of Frankish spearmen round them; in front an officer in a red cloak speaks up to a Frisian standing in a small open boat; behind, one ferry barge loading and the far bank low and green.
Five in the sheep house

Tetta brings you to the sheep house after dark, with no light. Behind the hurdles, among the ewes, sit a man, his wife, his old mother, a boy of twelve and a small girl. They are Saxons, with marsh mud dried on them to the hip. The man stands up when you come in. The others do not move at all.
They came over the flats two nights ago at low water, carrying the old woman. I have had stranger lodgers, but none so quiet. His name is Meginward. He has silver on his arm and no boat.
You have been up the Rhine. Then you have seen where the rest of them are going, and I need not tell you why these five would sooner sit with my sheep.
We are from Wihmodia, between the Weser and the Elbe. When the count's riders came to count us onto the road we were in the reeds. Eleven nights from there to here. We ate what the tide left.
My brother Meginfrid went to the Danes six summers ago, after the fight on the Sventana. He has a boat and a hearth there. Set us on the Danes' strand and he will pay you what I cannot.
You have seen the people on the road. Was there a woman called Ricburg, with a mark on her cheek like a thumb? No. Do not tell me now. Tell me when we are at sea.

Know what you are doing before you do it. The count keeps a boat of twelve oars at the river mouth, and they look under sails. A man who carries Saxons out is a man who has broken the emperor's order.
Take them aboard on the night tide, for Ripa
Pay Tetta for their keep and say you will think on it
Tell them you carry cloth, not people

Meginward lays his arm on the hurdle and cuts a finger's length from his arm ring with his own knife: eighteen pennies' weight. They come down to the creek in the dark holding each other's clothes. The old woman is lifted in last and sits on the cloth like a bale. Five people is most of what the boat will carry.

Tetta takes the ten pennies and says that for that they can have milk as well. Meginward says nothing. He has heard men say they will think on it before. They stay behind the hurdles, and you have a few days.

Meginward nods, as at a price he expected. The woman pulls the girl's hood down over her face. Tetta walks you back to the creek and says only that the tide is at the fourth hour, in case cloth should change its mind.

Inside a low turf-walled sheep house at night, lit only by moonlight through the door: a tall fair Saxon stands among the ewes, a silver ring on his upper arm; behind wattle hurdles his wife, an old woman, a boy and a small girl sit close together, mud to the hip; a stout Frisian woman in the doorway and the merchant beside her, seen from behind.
The count's man counts heads

At the toll post a Frank with six spearmen reads the emperor's order to every shipman on the creek. He reads it badly, from memory, with a clerk's tablet held up for show. Then he asks each man alone what he has seen. His name is Gundhart, and he does not like the coast.
Every Saxon of Wihmodia and of the land over the Elbe, man, woman and child, goes into Francia by the emperor's word. Not most of them. All. I have a number to bring to the road, and I am short.

A man who finds me one has his share by the head, paid at the count's court when the count sits. It is honest silver. Nobody is harmed by it. They are fed on the road, which is more than they were in the reeds.
A man who carries one out of the realm has carried off what is the emperor's. He answers for it with his goods, and the boat is goods.
You I have heard of. You lent your hull on the Rhine when it was asked for. Good. Then you know these people are not hard to count once they are sitting down.
So, shipman. This is a small mound in a great deal of mud. A stranger here is seen by somebody. What have you seen?
Tell him: five, in the sheep house on the mound
You carry cloth. You have seen sheep
Give him something for his trouble on this wet coast

He sends four spearmen up the mound and stays to make his mark on the clerk's tablet, five strokes and your name. There is no noise from the sheep house. They walk down between the spears, the old woman carried. Tetta stands in her door and looks at you until you look somewhere else. Your share is to be had at the count's court, a season on.
He looks at your cloth, lifts a corner, and lets it fall. Sheep, he says, there are plenty of. He goes on up the coast with his six men and says he will be back with the spring tide.

He looks at you longer than at your cloth. Sheep, he says. He has the clerk write your name and the look of your boat, the patch on the sail and all. Then he goes on up the coast, and says he will be back with the spring tide.

Thirty pennies go into his glove without either of you looking at them. He says a man could count this coast for a year and still be short, and that he will begin at the far end of it. Your toll on this creek is lighter for a month.

A timber toll post on a muddy creek bank under low grey cloud: a Frank in a wet red cloak faces the merchant, one gloved hand held out flat; a clerk behind him holds up a wax tablet; six spearmen stand about, bored; on the green mound behind, small and far off, a sheep house with its door shut.
The guard boat

A boat of twelve oars pulls out from under the bank and a man in her bow holds a spear up crosswise: stop. The five are lying on the bottom boards under the spare sail. The small girl has her mother's hand over her mouth. The ebb is running, and to seaward the flats are beginning to show brown.
Frisian boat! Lower your yard and lie to. The count's watch. What is under the sail?
We look in every hull that leaves this river until the counting is done. If you carry cloth, you lose a little of the tide. If you carry Saxons, you lose more than that.
A boat with a patch on her sail, shaped like a boot. I was told to look out for one.
Heave to and let them look, with the cloth piled on the sail
Run over the flats on the ebb: she draws more than you
Put about for Emuthon before she is near, and set them ashore again

A spearman steps aboard and walks on the cloth. He lifts two bolts, finds a third under them, and is tired of cloth. Under his feet nobody breathes. The captain waves you on. When the guard boat is small astern the old woman says one word in Saxon, and the boy laughs and is hit for it.

The spearman steps on the sail and the sail has a foot in it. They are lifted out one by one into the guard boat, the old woman last. The captain fines you forty pennies on the spot and has your name. Meginward looks back once. He does not look angry. That is worse. They will go into the column on the Rhine road, where a priest might still ask for them.

You put the helm up and go where the water is the colour of ale. The keel touches twice and comes free. The guard boat follows as far as the first bank and stops there with her oars in the air. Somebody aboard her will know your sail again.

You put the helm up and go where the water is the colour of ale, and then where it is the colour of mud. She sits down on a bank with the ebb leaving her. The guard boat waits in the channel for the tide to do her work, then sends men across the sand on foot. They take the five, and a mate's tooth for his manners. They will go into the column on the Rhine road, where a priest might still ask for them.

You go about while there is still half a mile between you, like a man who has forgotten something. The guard boat watches you all the way in and does not follow. The five go back up the mound by the sheep path. Tetta says nothing, loudly.

A broad river mouth on a falling tide, early morning, grey and windy: a Frankish guard boat of twelve oars pulling across the bow of a small open Frisian boat, a man in her bow holding a spear crosswise over his head; in the small boat four crewmen and a heap of cloth and sail, a child's hand just showing under the sail's edge; brown sand flats drying to seaward.
The night after

The count's man has gone up the coast and will be back with the next spring tide. Tetta has thought about it over her spinning, and says the sheep house will not hide five people twice. Meginward sits on an upturned trough with his knife and his arm ring on his knee, waiting to hear what he is worth.
Nine days to the spring tide. Then he comes back and counts my sheep, and he can count that far. They go before then, or they stop being Saxons.
And he has your sail written down. I would sew a new patch on it. A different shape.

There is the priest. Liudger. He is one of ours, a Frisian, and the emperor has set him over the western Saxons as well. He is up the river at Daventre or on the Ruhr this season. If any man can ask for five Saxons in daylight, he can.
North to my brother, if you will. If not that, anywhere they do not count. I can herd, plough, thatch and keep quiet. My wife weaves. The boy can learn anything that does not need reading.
You said cloth, not people. I did not hold it against you. A man has one boat. I ask again because I have nobody else to ask.
Whichever way you take them by water, mind the guard boat. Twelve oars, at the mouth, and up the river another like it. They look under sails.
Take them north to the Danes, tonight
Take them up the river to the priest Liudger
Make Frisians of them: the outer terp, Tetta's name, and your silver for their keep

Meginward cuts eighteen pennies' weight from his arm ring and holds it out on the flat of the knife. They come down to the creek in the dark holding each other's clothes. Tetta gives the girl a cheese to hold, so that she has something to do with her hands.

It is the long way and the one that can be spoken of afterwards. They go aboard before light. Meginward asks if the priest is the kind who asks what a man ate in Lent. Tetta says he is the kind who asks, and then feeds you.

Tetta had a brother who went out to the island of Bant and died there with his name still good. These are now his people, come home. Meginward gets a Frisian cloak, a crook and forty of somebody else's sheep on the outer terp. He is told to talk as little as he likes. That, he says, he can do.

A Frisian house on the terp at night, a peat fire and one tallow light: a stout woman spinning on a bench, speaking; the Saxon father on an upturned trough with a knife and a silver arm ring on his knee; in the shadow behind him his family asleep in a heap of fleeces; the merchant by the door with his cloak still on.
Whose guests are these

The five stand on the strand among the booths, in everybody's way. An old Dane with a staff comes down and looks them over like a cargo nobody has claimed. He asks, through a boy who has some Frisian, who answers for them here.
A man with no host here is a thing found on the beach. Anyone may pick up what he finds. I would be sorry to see it. I have seen it.

Meginfrid the Saxon? He is a real man, and he has a hearth here. But he is at Sliesthorp with his boat, like every man who has one. The king is there with the fleet and all the horsemen, looking at the emperor over a river.
Meginfrid the Saxon? He is a real man, and he has a hearth here. He is away east with his boat after furs. A month, if the wind likes him.
Until he comes, somebody of standing says before me: these are mine, I answer for what they do and for what is done to them. That is all the law there is to it. It is enough.
I have half an arm ring and five mouths. I am not much of a guest.
Answer for them yourself until the brother comes
Pay a householder to take them under his roof
You were paid to the strand. Here is the strand

You say it before him, in Frisian, and the boy says it after you in Danish with more words than you used. The old man strikes the sand once with his staff. They are yours until the brother comes. The booth-holders stop looking at the girl. The talk on the strand is all of the king's fleet lying at the Slie.

A comb maker with a wide house takes twenty-four pennies' weight and the five of them, and says the old woman can have the place by the fire because his own mother is dead and it is empty. The lawman is content. The talk on the strand is all of the king's fleet lying at the Slie.

You push off. They stand where the boat was, the water filling the mark of her keel. The old man with the staff watches you go and then, since somebody must, says a short thing in Danish and takes them up the bank himself. The talk on the strand, behind you, is all of the king's fleet lying at the Slie.

A Danish market strand at midday under a high pale sky: plank booths and beached boats; the five Saxons standing close together on the sand with one bundle; an old Dane with a long staff and a silver-ringed cloak pin faces the merchant, a boy between them turning his head from one to the other; booth-holders watching.
What the Frisian saw

Meginfrid has come: a Saxon in a Dane's cloak, older and broader than his brother, with a purse for you. With him is a man with gold on his arm who speaks for the king. The king wants to hear, from somebody with no side in it, what the Franks are doing with the Saxons.
You carried five of my blood past the count's boat in a hull I would not put a pig in. I do not have words for that in any of my three tongues. I have this.
They tell me you left them on the sand with nobody to speak for them. I will pay what my brother promised. Take it. A debt is a debt.

The emperor's men have come over the border about people like these. They say: give back what ran to you. The king lies at Sliesthorp with the ships and has not gone to their meeting. Before he answers he would know what he is asked to give back, and to what.
The summer the emperor emptied the land, his men asked the king to give back what ran to him. The king remembers being asked. He would know what became of the ones who did not run.
You trade on the Franks' rivers. You have eyes. Say what you saw. Nobody will hear who said it.

There is one thing more, and it is not the king's business. My brother says our father's brother's people did not come in to be counted either. Forty of them, in the reeds by the Jade, when he left. Forty is not a thing I can ask of a man with one small boat.
Tell it as you saw it, on the Rhine and on the Ems
You are a guest here and the emperor's man at home: you saw the weather
Offer to go back for the forty in the reeds

You tell it flat: the bank, the counting, the children held by the wrist, the land given to the Wends. The king's man listens without moving his face and at the end unties a bundle of forty marten skins and lays it by your knee. It is said afterwards that the king gave nobody back. Meginfrid's purse holds sixty pennies' weight of cut silver.

The king's man says that a merchant who sees only weather will live to be old, and gets up. Meginfrid waits until he has gone and then laughs, once. His purse holds eighty pennies' weight of cut silver, and he counts it into your hand piece by piece, like a man paying a wergild.

Meginfrid looks at you for some time. Then he puts eighty pennies' weight in your hand as earnest and tells you what his brother told him: a reed island at the edge of the Jade, two tides east of the Ems, where the gulls nest. Ask at Emuthon for a pilot who knows the gullies. The king's man says that the king likes a man who finishes what he starts.

Inside a Danish booth by the water in the evening, a small fire and the door open on masts: a broad Saxon in a Danish cloak holds out a purse to the merchant; beside him sits a still, well-dressed Dane with gold arm rings and a bundle of dark marten skins at his feet; outside, in the dusk, the younger brother's family sits round a pot.
Forty in the reeds

Folcger the pilot has been out to look, in an eel boat, as a man after eels. They are there: forty people on a reed island at the edge of the Jade, two tides east of here, eating mussels and gulls' eggs. They have a fire they light only in fog. Your boat holds five.
I counted forty-one. One is very new. They thought I was the count's man and were going to drown me. Then I said your Saxon's name, and his father's, and they gave me an egg.
Forty-one people, five to a boat like yours. You can do that sum. Eight runs and a bit, two tides each way. That is four nights if nothing goes wrong, and on four nights something goes wrong.
The guard boat rows the coast every third night and does not say which. One run she will not see. Eight runs she will. I tell you this now so that you cannot say afterwards that nobody did.
And they know your sail. I would not show it east of the mound at all.

Or: my cousins have three eel boats, deep ones, and no love for a Frank who counts their catch. One night, one tide, all forty to a ship's side off the islands, and your Saxon's Danes take them from there. Ninety pennies between us. For that we were never born.
Hire Folcger and three eel boats: one night, one tide
Do it with your own boat: eight runs, four nights
Forty is a levy, not a cargo. Send them word of the road and no more

A night with no moon and a little rain, which Folcger says he ordered. Four boats go in on the flood with muffled oars and come out on the ebb low in the water and silent, even the new one. Off the outer island a Danish hull is lying with no light, Meginfrid in her bow. By morning there are four eel boats on the creek, full of eels.

Four nights. Eight times in over the flats and eight times out, five and six at a time, to a Danish hull lying off the outer island. On the last run the guard boat passes so near that you hear a man in her complain of his supper. The crew do not speak of it afterwards, except to each other, often.

Three nights go well. On the fourth the guard boat is lying in the gully with her oars shipped, waiting. You get clear over a bank she cannot cross, with one man hurt by a thrown spear and nobody aboard but your own. Twenty-two came out. Nineteen are still in the reeds, and now the count knows where the reeds are.

Folcger carries the word out with his eel traps: the Ems, the sheep house, the name of the Danes' strand, and that nobody is coming. He says they heard it without complaint. He says that people who complain do not last long enough in a reed bed to hear news.

The creek at Emuthon at dusk, low water: a lean weathered Frisian pilot squats on the mud beside an eel boat, drawing channels in the mud with a stick for the merchant; three more eel boats drawn up behind; far to the east over the flats a line of reeds under a darkening sky.
The priest asks for them

Liudger hears it through without a word, walking, leading his horse. Then he says that the emperor's order tells where Saxons may not live. It does not tell whose land they must live on. He has land on the Ruhr, at Werden, and not enough hands on it.
Five, in your boat, at this bank. Then bring them up to the church before somebody counts them for me. Nobody is taken from Lebuin's door. Not even by a count's man in a hurry.
Taken from your boat and put in the column. Then they are on the Rhine road, and I know which clerk at Colonia holds the lists. A name can be found on a list. It is what lists are for.

They are to be settled among Christians, far from their woods, where they can do no harm and learn some good. Werden is among Christians. It is four days' walk from their woods, which I grant is not far. I will not measure it if the count does not.
I am a priest with a wide parish and a king's letter, no more. The count need not listen to me. But he was baptised by a man I taught, and he knows it.
They have made me a bishop since Lent, at Mimigernaford, over the western Saxons. I did not ask for it. It turns out to be useful. A count answers a bishop's letter.

It will cost something. The count's man is paid by the head, and he will want his heads' worth from somebody. The Church can pay, slowly, after letters. Or a man can lay the silver down today and have God for a debtor, who is slow as well, but sure.
Lay down the count's price for five heads yourself
Carry his letter to the count and let the Church pay
Swear for them before him: they will work Werden's land, and you answer if they run

A hundred and twenty pennies, counted onto the church step. Liudger does not thank you. He writes your name in the book where the dead and the givers are prayed for, which he says will last longer. Then he has a leaf of the vow copied for you, the one every Saxon has had to say. Know, he says, what was asked of them before you judge how they answered.

He writes it standing, on his saddle, in a hand like a hedge, and seals it with a ring that is too big for him. It goes to the count by your boat. He asks, since you are going that way, for four cakes of wax for the altar, at a fair price and a little over. An answer will take until the next feast but one.

You swear it with your hand on the book: they will work the land at Werden and keep the peace, and if they run you answer for them with your goods. Liudger has a leaf of the vow copied for you, the one every Saxon has had to say, and reads you the Latin at the head of it twice over until some of it stays.

A river bank path below a timber church on a bright cold day: a tall spare tonsured man of sixty in a travel-stained cloak, a book satchel on his shoulder, leads a horse and listens with his head bent to the merchant walking beside him; behind them the small boat at the bank and Saxon converts and Frankish soldiers going up to the same church door.
The list

Gundhart is back on the creek, older and wetter, with a clerk and a list: the people of Wihmodia who were never counted onto the road. Somebody has told him of a shepherd on the outer terp whose Frisian is odd. Meginward's boy, Folcward, is fourteen now and as tall as you. He has been waiting for your sail since Easter.

Two winters the clerks have been at it. Every household of the district, from the old tithe rolls, and against each one a stroke if it reached the road. There are households with no stroke. One of them is a man, a wife, a mother, a boy, a girl.
And you I have written down already, shipman, from the first time. The boat with the patch. You see a great many sheep.
You were open-handed once before on this creek. I have not forgotten it. I say so only so that we understand each other.

He is my brother's man from Bant, and he talks like that because everybody on Bant talks like that. It comes of living on a sandbank with seals. I will swear it. I will bring six of my neighbours to swear it with me. That is our law, and it was our law before there were counts.
I can row and I can splice, and I can say every Frisian word there is for mud. Father says I may go if you will have me. He says a boy who is at sea cannot be counted.
And the women have something for you. Three bolts, two winters' weaving, on my loom. Do not say no to it. They have been looking for a way to stop owing you.
Swear beside Tetta that they are her dead brother's people
Say nothing, and move them to the island of Bant before he walks out there
Pay him to find the list complete

Eight people swear on the tide sand with the water coming in, which shortens the pleading. Gundhart knows what a Frisian oath is worth in a Frisian court. He has the clerk make a stroke: gone to Bant, dead. The boy comes aboard with a bundle and a new knife, and the three bolts go in under the thwart.

Eight people swear, and Gundhart asks the shepherd to say the Our Father in Frisian. He says it in something. The oath stands, because eight is eight, but Gundhart fines you thirty pennies for wasting a court and writes a long line beside your name. That night the family goes out to Bant in an eel boat. The boy comes with you instead, with the three bolts.

A night's work with the tide. By the time Gundhart has walked out to the outer terp in the morning there are forty sheep on it and a deaf old Frisian who has herded them, he says, since the flood. Bant is a low island with a chapel and nothing else, and nobody rows there to count. The boy comes aboard with the three bolts.

Forty pennies. Gundhart has the clerk make a stroke against a household of five and says the marsh takes a great many people and returns very few. He does not say goodbye. The boy comes aboard with a bundle, and the three bolts go in under the thwart.

The tide sand below the terp at Emuthon, a windy morning with the water coming in: a greying Frank in a red cloak and a clerk with a long parchment roll face a stout Frisian woman with six neighbours ranked behind her; to one side a tall fair boy of fourteen with a bundle stands by the merchant's beached boat; sheep on the far mound.
Saxons under a Danish roof

There is a new long house behind the booths with smoke coming through the thatch, and Saxon is spoken in it. The girl, Gerburg, is carrying water and scolding a goose in Danish. The brothers have set a bench for you by the fire. They have something to say about what is owed.
The king gave nobody back. He said a guest is a guest. He also said that Saxons who can ride are worth feeding, which is nearer his reason. We do not mind his reason.
Five of us, under a roof, uncounted. The old woman has a place by the fire. When they ask me in this country who my people are, I say your name after my father's. That is how it is done here.

Forty-six of us now, with the new one. A whole kin, with its old men and its quarrels. We have held a meeting, as our fathers did by the Weser and as the king's law forbade us. The meeting talked of you for most of a day.
Twenty-two came out. Nineteen went onto the road with the rest. It is not what you meant. It is twenty-two more than there were. We do not count it the way the count would.
They know your sail on the Frisian coast now, the count's people. That is a cost, and it came of our business. We have reckoned it in.

Here you are a guest for as long as any of us has a door: I have said it before the lawman, and it holds for your son. For the rest, there is silver. Or there is more than silver, if you want a thing that lasts.
Lay your hand to Meginfrid's: one purse, two boats
Take what they have weighed out, and their word
Leave them their silver: ask for a booth place on the bank beside theirs

It is done the Danes' way, hands laid together over a ring before the whole kin. One purse: what his boat earns in the east and yours in the west is shared at the year's end. The kin lay down their first share at once, nine hundred pennies' weight and four bundles of marten, gathered among forty-six people who came out of a reed bed with nothing. Meginfrid's boat is yours to send as your own.

Five hundred and twenty pennies' weight of cut silver, weighed twice on a folding scale, and a bundle of marten on top because the old woman said so. Meginfrid says a Saxon pays his debts so that he can afford his grudges. You have guest right here under his roof, and so will whoever comes after you.

Meginfrid walks you down the bank and paces out a booth's breadth next to his own, and the lawman drives a peg at each corner. The brothers will not let you go with nothing in the hold: five bundles of marten, the best of a winter's trading. A neighbour, Meginward says, is a thing his family had run out of.

Inside a new timber long house in the evening, firelight: two fair brothers, one in a Danish cloak, face the merchant across the hearth, a folding scale and cut silver on a bench between them; an old woman wrapped by the fire, a small girl with a water pail and a goose at the door; many faces along the walls if the forty came, few if they did not.
Counted onto the road

Gundhart has come from the count's court with a clerk and a bag. The five were counted onto the road with the last column before the frost. He has your share, and the count's good word if you want that more. He is in a good humour. His number came out right.
Five strokes, and your name against them. The clerks at Colonia were pleased. A household entire is neater on a list than odd heads.
They go west, a long way, to some abbey's land on the Seine, I think. Among Christians and vineyards. In ten years the children will speak like Neustrians and thank the emperor. So I am told.
That is twice you have been of use in this business, on the Rhine and here. The count remembers a name he hears twice.
The share is in the bag. Or the count will put his mark to something for you in place of part of it. A man who is known to be the count's man lands easier on this coast.

One thing, and I say it as a friend. The man looked at your boat a long time from the road. They are a people who remember, the Saxons. It is most of what they have left. I would hire no Saxon oars for a while.
Take the bag, and the name of count's shipman
Take less silver and a toll-free landing on this creek, in writing
Take the least, and ask that the five be set down on one piece of land together

Nine hundred pennies, new ones, with the emperor's name round the cross. Gundhart says before the toll man and the clerk that you are the count's shipman and are to be dealt with as one. Tetta sells you bread that evening at the stranger's price. The crew are quiet at the oars, and somebody has cut a small mark in the stem post that nobody will own to.

Six hundred pennies, and a strip of parchment with the count's mark: no toll on what you sell on this creek, for your life and your heir's. The toll man reads it with his lips moving. Tetta sells you bread that evening at the stranger's price. Somebody has cut a small mark in the stem post that nobody will own to.

Gundhart is surprised, and then not. He has the clerk write it: the household entire, to one holding, not to be parted. It costs you a third of the bag and he thinks you a fool, kindly. Six hundred pennies. It is said later that on abbey land by Rotomagus there is a row of huts, and in one of them five Saxons who speak to nobody. One of the men asks every ship for the Weser.

The toll post on the creek on a clear frosty morning: the Frank in the red cloak, pleased, sets a heavy leather bag on the toll bench before the merchant while a clerk unrolls a parchment; in a house door up the mound a Frisian woman stands with folded arms; on the small boat's stem post, close in the foreground, a fresh knife-cut mark.
Werden's people

The count has answered: five Saxons more or less on the bishop's land are the bishop's business. Meginward stands at the landing in a clean tunic with a tally stick in his belt, counting casks for the abbey. Liudger has the look of a man who has won a small case and means to enjoy it for a week.

The count writes that he has no objection, in eleven lines, nine of them about his own piety. They are on Werden's land, in a house that had no roof at Easter and has one now. The old woman has found fault with the well. I take that for a good sign.
You laid down the price when the Church was still looking for its purse. I told you God was a slow debtor and a sure one. He has been quicker than I said. I am almost put out.
You swore for them, and they have not run. They have not so much as walked fast. You may have your oath back, with interest.

It is not the Weser. The ground is hard and it stays where you leave it. But I have ploughed it, and my mother will be buried in it under a cross with her own name. The bishop asked what I could do besides plough. I said I could count without a clerk.
When they lifted us out of your boat I thought, there, that is the end of that Frisian. Then the priest came down the column with your name in his mouth. I had the wrong end.

Now, what is owed. The abbey pays its debts in what it has: wax, honey, and its good word, which opens doors on this river. And Meginward keeps our landing here. He could keep a merchant's goods beside ours, if the merchant were one we knew.
Take back your silver with the Church's thanks, the bishop's hand over your house, and Meginward at the landing
Ask for the bishop's hand over your house
Ask for Meginward at the landing, to keep your goods with the abbey's

Liudger gives you everything he offered, and says a man who pays first should not be made to choose after. Four hundred and twenty pennies from the abbey's chest, ten cakes of wax, six crocks of Saxon honey. A letter under his seal says your house is under his hand, and the toll men of this river are to go gently with you for a year. Meginward takes your mark onto his tally stick, next to the abbey's.

A letter under the bishop's seal: this house and its boats are under his hand, and who wrongs them wrongs him. A count's man will read that twice before he lifts your cloth. With it go two hundred and sixty pennies and nine cakes of wax. Meginward carries them down to the boat himself and will not let the crew help.

Meginward takes your mark onto his tally stick, next to the abbey's. What you leave at this landing he will keep dry, count right, and sell when the price is good and not before. Ten cakes of wax, six crocks of honey and a hundred pennies go into the hold. He says he owes you five lives, and means to pay by the cask.

A river landing on a mild bright day, casks and wax cakes stacked on the bank: the Saxon father in a clean undyed tunic with a tally stick in his belt; the tall old bishop beside him, smiling a little, a sealed letter in his hand held out to the merchant; behind, the abbey's barge and a road going up a wooded valley.
The empty land

Six winters a Frisian shepherd, Meginward has heard what every shipman on the creek is saying. The Wends could not hold the north. The emperor's counts are building a fort on the far side of the Elbe. And on the Weser marsh, where the war is over at last, nobody is counting heads any more.

They gave our land to the Wends, and the Danes took it from the Wends, and now the Franks have taken it back and found nobody in it to pay a tithe. An empty land is no use to a count. He will not ask a man with a plough where he has been.

And this summer the Danes came here, two hundred ships, and took their silver from the Frisians by weight. Tetta paid with the rest. I stood on her mound with a crook and watched a king's fleet rob the people who hid me from an emperor. I am tired of other men's mounds.
They have sworn a peace on the Eider, twelve men from each side, I hear, with their hands on their swords. When great men swear peace, small men can go and look at their fields.

I will tell you a thing I have told nobody. Under my hearth stone there is a pot. My father's rings and mine, and the bride silver. I buried it the night before the riders came. The house is burned. A hearth stone does not burn.

And I say he is a fool. There is nothing there but nettles and that pot. Here he has forty sheep and a name. The girl is asked for by a man with his own boat. Fetch the pot by all means. Then come back and be Frisians. You are good at it by now.
We have lived on Bant, too, on a sandbank with a chapel. I have seen what the sea means to do with that island. I would sooner trust the Weser.
Carry them home, and buy them seed corn, an axe, a plough iron and a cow
Carry them home across the Jade on a quiet tide
Tell him what Tetta says: there is nothing there but his silver. Fetch it, and stay

Two tides east, then up a gully Meginward names turn by turn with his eyes shut. The house is a black square in the nettles. The hearth stone has not moved. He lifts the pot out, takes one ring for the girl's wedding, and pushes the rest across to you, eleven hundred pennies' weight. Then he takes off the arm ring he cut for your first passage, the cut still bright, and puts it on your arm. The cow goes ashore last, complaining. By harvest there is smoke on the Weser marsh, and by the next there are three smokes.

Two tides east, then up a gully Meginward names turn by turn with his eyes shut, so that you learn them too. The house is a black square in the nettles. The hearth stone has not moved. He counts out seven hundred pennies' weight from the pot and keeps the rest to begin again with. They stand on their own ground and watch you down the gully. The old woman is already pulling nettles.

He goes with you across the Jade and digs, and stands a while in the nettles with the pot under his arm. Then he comes back to the boat. He gives you three hundred and sixty pennies' weight of it. The women add six bolts of cloth. In the spring he buys the house next to Tetta's and takes your goods under his roof as his own. His grandchildren will say they were always Frisians. Nobody will write down that they were not.

A wide green marsh under a huge summer sky, a tidal gully with the small boat nosed into the bank: in the foreground the Saxon father, greyer now, kneels in nettles beside a blackened hearth stone tipped on its edge, lifting out a clay pot; his wife, old mother, tall son and grown daughter stand round him; a cow being led down a plank from the boat.

The Saxons of Wihmodia and from over the Elbe are being walked into Francia, whole households, and set down far apart. The land beyond the Elbe is given to the Wends. Grain and bread are dear along the Rhine road while the columns pass.

The king of the Danes has lain at Sliesthorp with his ships and all his horsemen, on the border of the Saxons. The emperor's men asked him to give back those who fled to him. Nobody has seen any given back.
